title: Descendant vs child selectors
why_it_matters: One symbol decides how deep a rule reaches.
explanation: A space between selectors matches any descendant at any depth. The > symbol matches only direct children. Use > when you want to style one level and leave nested elements alone.
try_it: Nest a link inside a sub-menu and see which of the two rules reaches it.

title: Attribute selectors style by HTML attributes
why_it_matters: You can target elements without adding classes.
explanation: Square brackets match elements by attribute. a[target="_blank"] picks links that open in a new tab, and input[type="email"] picks email fields. Add ^= for starts with, $= for ends with and *= for contains.
try_it: Make every link that ends in .pdf bold without adding a class.

title: The cascade picks winners in a set order
why_it_matters: Knowing the order ends the guessing when a style loses.
explanation: When rules conflict, the browser checks importance first, then cascade layers, then specificity, then source order. The first step that finds a difference decides the winner. Later steps are only used for ties.
try_it: Take a style that does not apply and walk through the four steps to find why it loses.

title: Pseudo-classes use one colon, elements two
why_it_matters: It tells you whether you style a state or a part.
explanation: A pseudo-class like :hover or :focus describes a state of the element. A pseudo-element like ::before or ::first-line styles a part of it. Modern CSS writes pseudo-elements with two colons.
try_it: Style the first line of a paragraph and the hover state of a button.

title: Common mistake: ::before without content
why_it_matters: It is why your generated element never appears.
explanation: A ::before or ::after element is only created if it has a content value. Without it, nothing renders, whatever else you set. Use content: "" for a decorative shape, then give it size and a background.
try_it: Draw a small red dot with ::after and make it appear.

title: :not() excludes elements
why_it_matters: It replaces rules you later have to undo.
explanation: :not() matches everything that does not fit the selector inside it. It is useful for a rule that applies to all items except one, so you do not have to write the rule and then reset it.
try_it: Put a divider between list items but not after the last one.

title: Before vs after: :is() shortens selector lists
why_it_matters: Repeated selectors collapse into one line.
explanation: :is() takes a list of selectors and matches any of them. It saves repeating the same parent for each child. Its specificity equals the most specific selector in the list, so keep that in mind.
try_it: Find a long comma-separated selector in your CSS and shorten it with :is().

title: :where() adds styles with zero specificity
why_it_matters: Base styles are easy to override later.
explanation: :where() works like :is() but always has zero specificity. Rules written with it never win a fight against your other rules. That makes it ideal for default styles in a reset or component library.
try_it: Override a :where() rule with a plain class and see that it wins without effort.

title: :has() selects a parent by its children
why_it_matters: CSS can finally style a parent based on what is inside.
explanation: :has() matches an element if it contains something that fits the selector inside. For example, .card:has(img) picks only cards that include an image. It is supported in all current major browsers.
try_it: Give cards with an image a two-column layout, and leave the others alone.

title: :has() reacts to form state
why_it_matters: You can style a wrapper when its input changes.
explanation: Combine :has() with state pseudo-classes to style a wrapper. .field:has(:focus-visible) highlights the whole field when its input has keyboard focus. It replaces small JavaScript snippets that toggle classes.
try_it: Make a checkbox label turn bold when its box is checked, with no JavaScript.

title: Specificity decides which rule wins
why_it_matters: It explains most why-is-my-style-ignored bugs.
explanation: Each selector has a weight. An ID beats a class, a class beats an element, and inline styles beat all of them. When two rules conflict, the more specific selector wins, whatever the order in the file.
try_it: Give one paragraph the class and ID above and predict its color before checking.

title: Quiz: which color wins, class or two elements?
why_it_matters: It checks you count specificity, not selector length.
explanation: Question: .note sets blue and div p sets red. A paragraph with the class note sits inside a div. Which color shows? Answer: blue. One class outweighs any number of element selectors.
code:
div p { color: red; }
.note { color: blue; }
try_it: Add a third element to the red selector and confirm blue still wins.

title: Common mistake: selectors that are too specific
why_it_matters: Overly long selectors are hard to override later.
explanation: A selector like nav ul li a.link has high specificity and ties your CSS to the HTML structure. Prefer one flat class, such as .nav-link. Then any later rule can override it without a fight.
try_it: Pick your longest selector and rewrite it as a single class.

title: Source order breaks specificity ties
why_it_matters: It tells you where to put an override.
explanation: If two rules have equal specificity, the one that appears later in the CSS wins. This is why overrides go after the base styles. Link order of stylesheets in the HTML matters too.
try_it: Swap the order of two equal rules and watch the winner change.

title: @layer sets the cascade order yourself
why_it_matters: You stop fighting third-party CSS.
explanation: Cascade layers let you declare an order, like reset, base and components. A rule in a later layer wins over an earlier layer, regardless of selector specificity. Declare the order once at the top.
try_it: Put third-party CSS in an early layer and your own styles in a later one.

title: Quiz: does layered or unlayered CSS win?
why_it_matters: It is the surprise that catches most beginners.
explanation: Question: one rule sits inside a layer, an identical conflicting rule sits outside any layer. Which wins? Answer: the unlayered rule, regardless of specificity. Unlayered styles come after all layers in the order.
try_it: Move the blue rule inside a layer declared before base and see red win.

title: Some properties inherit, some do not
why_it_matters: It explains why text styles flow down but borders do not.
explanation: Text properties like color, font-family and line-height pass from parent to child automatically. Layout properties like margin, padding and border do not. Set text styles once on body and children follow.
try_it: Set a color on body and check which child elements follow it in DevTools.

title: inherit, initial and unset
why_it_matters: Three keywords reset or copy any property.
explanation: inherit copies the parent's value, initial uses the property's default from the spec and unset acts as inherit for inherited properties and initial for the rest. Useful for resetting buttons and links.
try_it: Make links take their color from the surrounding text using color: inherit.

title: CSS nesting groups related rules
why_it_matters: Component styles live in one block, as in Sass.
explanation: Native CSS nesting lets you write child rules inside a parent. Use & for the parent itself, such as &:hover. It works in all current major browsers and needs no build step.
try_it: Rewrite one component's CSS so its child and hover rules are nested inside it.

title: See why a rule loses in the Styles panel
why_it_matters: DevTools shows the exact winner and the losers.
explanation: Select an element and open the Styles panel. Rules that lose are crossed out, and the winning rule sits above them. Hover the selector to see its specificity, and tick or untick declarations to test changes.
try_it: Find a struck-through declaration in DevTools and work out which rule beat it.

title: Custom properties store reusable values
why_it_matters: Change a brand color in one place.
explanation: A custom property starts with two dashes and is read with var(). Define them on :root to share them everywhere. A second value in var() acts as a fallback if the property is missing.
try_it: Replace a repeated color in your CSS with one custom property.

title: Custom properties can change per component
why_it_matters: They cascade, so themes become a few lines.
explanation: Custom properties inherit like color does. Redefine one on a class and everything inside uses the new value. This is how a dark theme or a danger button variant can be written in a few lines.
try_it: Add class dark to a parent and watch every .panel inside it change.

title: @property gives a custom property a type
why_it_matters: The browser can animate it smoothly.
explanation: Normally a custom property is just text, so transitions on it jump. @property declares a type, such as an angle, plus an initial value. Then the browser understands it and can animate it between values.
try_it: Use --angle in a conic-gradient and transition it on hover.

title: A small reset to start every project
why_it_matters: It removes browser differences without hiding useful defaults.
explanation: A short reset makes projects consistent. Use border-box sizing, remove the default body margin and make media elements fit their container. Avoid huge resets that remove everything, because then you rebuild it all.
try_it: Paste this reset at the top of a new project and compare it before and after.

title: Project idea: a theme switcher with variables
why_it_matters: It combines custom properties, inheritance and selectors.
explanation: Build a page with a light and a dark theme using only custom properties. Define the colors on :root and override them under a class on the html element. Add a button that toggles the class.
try_it: List five color variables you need, then write both themes before adding the button.
